The MacBook Air M5 is the best overall pick for many computer science students because it combines portability, battery life, quiet operation, strong everyday performance, and a clean macOS development environment. It is easy to carry around campus, comfortable for lectures, and strong enough for coding, research, web development, documents, notes, video calls, and general student use.

For computer science students who work with Python, JavaScript, web development, Git, VS Code, terminals, browser tabs, documentation, and general programming assignments, the MacBook Air M5 can be an excellent choice.

...

The main warning is course compatibility. Some computer science courses, engineering tools, cybersecurity labs, or Windows-only applications may be easier on a Windows laptop. Before buying a Mac, check your university’s software requirements and ask whether Windows is required for any modules.

If your course is mostly coding, web development, Python, Java, databases, and general software work, the MacBook Air M5 is one of the easiest laptops to recommend.

...

The Lenovo ThinkPad T14 Gen 6 is the best Windows laptop here for computer science students who want a practical, reliable, work-focused machine for coding, Linux learning, virtual machines, documentation, browser tabs, and long study sessions.

For CS students, the keyboard is a serious advantage. You may spend hours writing code, debugging, taking notes, writing reports, using terminals, searching documentation, and switching between lectures, assignments, and browser tabs. A comfortable keyboard can matter more than a slightly thinner design.

The ThinkPad T14 Gen 6 is especially useful if your course involves Windows tools, Linux environments, virtual machines, databases, cybersecurity labs, Microsoft software, remote desktops, or business-style development workflows.

A 16GB RAM configuration can work for many students, but 32GB RAM is the better long-term choice if you plan to run virtual machines, Android Studio, local databases, multiple IDEs, many browser tabs, or heavier final-year projects.

...

The ThinkPad P14s Gen 6 is the best choice here for computer science students who expect heavier workloads. It makes sense if your course includes virtual machines, cybersecurity labs, software testing environments, data projects, engineering tools, technical research, or larger programming projects.

Compared with a normal student laptop, the ThinkPad P14s feels more like a compact workstation-style machine. That can be useful if your laptop needs to run a host operating system, Linux VMs, Windows test machines, code editors, browsers, terminals, databases, and notes at the same time.

This laptop is not necessary for every first-year student. If you are mostly doing basic programming and web development, the MacBook Air, ThinkPad T14, Zenbook 14, or Dell XPS 13 may be enough. But if you want more headroom for technical labs, the ThinkPad P14s Gen 6 is the strongest pick in this guide.

...

For computer science students, the most important specs are RAM, processor performance, SSD storage, keyboard comfort, screen quality, battery life, portability, and operating system compatibility.

For basic programming and first-year coding, 16GB RAM is a sensible minimum. For heavier coursework, Android Studio, virtual machines, local databases, cybersecurity labs, data projects, Docker-style workflows, or many browser tabs, 32GB RAM is a better long-term choice.

Storage matters too. A 512GB SSD can work for many students, but 1TB is safer if you keep virtual machines, SDKs, datasets, projects, course videos, notes, backups, and large development environments on the laptop.

...

The best laptop for computer science students in 2026 depends on your course requirements, budget, operating system preference, and how heavy your coding workload will become.

Choose the MacBook Air M5 if you want the easiest overall laptop for coding, portability, battery life, notes, lectures, and general student use.

Choose the Lenovo ThinkPad T14 Gen 6 if you want the safest Windows laptop for computer science, coding, Linux learning, virtual machines, and serious productivity.

Choose the ThinkPad P14s Gen 6 if you expect heavier CS labs, virtual machines, cybersecurity work, software testing, or technical projects.

Choose the MacBook Pro 14 if you want a premium Mac with stronger performance and a better screen than the MacBook Air.

Choose the ASUS Zenbook 14 if you want a portable, premium-feeling Windows laptop with good value, depending on the deal.

Choose the Dell XPS 13 if you want a sleek, compact Windows laptop for coding and student productivity.

## What computer science students actually need

Memory first. An IDE like VS Code or IntelliJ, a browser full of documentation, Slack or Discord, and a local server easily use 8GB on their own. With 16GB you’re comfortable; with 32GB you can add virtual machines and containers.

A Unix-like environment. Upper-level courses assume a Linux-style terminal. macOS gives you one natively. On Windows, install WSL2 to run Ubuntu alongside Windows — it’s free and well supported.

Battery life and keyboard. You’ll spend hours typing in labs and libraries. A comfortable keyboard and a laptop that lasts all day matter more than benchmark scores.

Storage. 512GB is enough for most students. Developer tools, Docker images and datasets grow quickly, so avoid 256GB if you can.

## Mac, Windows or Linux for computer science?

| If you… | Choose |
| --- | --- |
| Want the smoothest terminal and long battery life | MacBook Air or MacBook Pro |
| Need Windows-only tools (.NET desktop apps, some game engines) | Intel or AMD Windows laptop with WSL2 |
| Plan to train models with CUDA | Windows laptop with an NVIDIA RTX GPU |
| Want to run Linux natively | Intel or AMD laptop (dual-boot) |

## Thinking about a $2,000–$3,000 laptop with a dedicated GPU?

Some students search for a high-end GPU laptop for computer science. It’s only worth it if you’ll train neural networks locally, do graphics research, or game seriously. If so, look for an NVIDIA RTX laptop GPU with at least 8GB of video memory, 32GB of system memory and a 1TB SSD, and accept a heavier laptop and shorter battery life. For everyone else, a MacBook Air or a 32GB ultrabook plus your university’s GPU cluster is a better use of the money.

title: Best Laptops for College Students (2026): MacBooks and Beyond | WIRED
text:
### MacBook Neo

...

The MacBook Air (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is my choice for best overall laptop for everyone. But college students have specific needs—and often, specific budgets. In addition to being affordable, a college student’s laptop should be lightweight and easy to carry around. The MacBook Neo (7/10, WIRED Recommends) fits the bill perfectly. It’s only 2.7 pounds and starts at just $699. It also has a smaller display, which helps it fit on those tiny lecture-hall desks. What makes the MacBook Neo special, however, is its lack of compromise around quality. It’s a gorgeous piece of hardware, with fun colors, an excellent trackpad, a beautiful display, and that Apple “it” factor. I recommend the $699 model, which gets you twice the storage and a Touch ID fingerprint reader.

Of course, this isn’t a laptop without downsides. Apple invested its efforts in the front-of-screen experience, but made cuts to performance, ports, and memory to keep costs low. The limitation of 8 GB of memory is my biggest sticking point with this device; it means you’ll need to be mindful of how many applications, tabs, and background tasks you have running at once. Also, ghe Neo can connect to only one external display at a time.

...

Laptop pricing has skyrocketed over the past few months, which has made it harder to recommend some of the flashier new laptops of the year. Fortunately, many really great laptops from 2025 are still available to buy. The Dell 14 Plus is a great example. It’s one of the few laptops you can get for less than $1,000 that doesn’t force you to make serious compromises. It’s not the world’s prettiest device, but the display is surprisingly sharp, bright, and colorful. The computer’s touchpad and keyboard are both high-quality, and it has tons of ports.

The newer Dell 14S came out more recently with the intention to replace the 14 Plus. The new model comes with an OLED display and superb battery life. While it’s a solid option (see Other Laptops to Consider, below), it starts at a pricey $1,350, and the screen has a lower resolution. For a college student, the Dell 14 Plus is the better buy right now.

...

I tested the HP OmniBook 3 and found that it shares a lot of the positive qualities of its older sibling. The OLED screen is great, as is the keyboard and overall build quality. Most important, the battery life is top-notch for a device of this price.

...

However, Chromebooks are still the way to go if you need something— anything—for as little money as possible. If you’re low on cash and just need basic internet access, the $200 Asus Chromebook CX15 is your best bet. The screen and touchpad are the main downfalls, but it’s fairly portable and modern-looking, and the battery life is decent enough. My bar is fairly low for a $200 laptop, but the CX15 outdoes other competitors at this price.

...

### LOQ 15

Lenovo (RTX 5050, 512 GB)

Not everyone needs a powerful laptop to tote around campus. But if you’re in a STEM field, or even just like to play games on the weekend, buying a single, powerful laptop to serve as your main machine at college is a good idea. Unfortunately, no gaming laptop is powerful, portable, and affordable—you can only have two of those three things. Letting go of the portability priority, the best option I’ve tested is the Lenovo LOQ 15 (8/10, WIRED Recommends). It’s hard to beat a discrete graphics processing unit (GPU) for raw performance, which is exactly what the RTX 5060 in the LOQ 15 delivers. Though the price often creeps above $1,000, it’s still the most affordable gaming laptop you can buy that doesn’t suffer from severe performance compromises.

...

Razer

Now, if you can afford to dish out some more money, I’d point you to either the Razer Blade 16 or the MacBook Pro. Despite the thin profile of the Razer Blade 16 (8/10 WIRED Recommends), you can configure it with up to an RTX 5090 graphics card. Aside from the compromise of a high price, battery life is a limitation. You might run out halfway through your day, forcing you to find an outlet in a hurry. If you happen to need performance for gaming on the weekends in addition to your schoolwork, the Razer Blade 16 is expensive but totally worth it.
